scenes.title: Where and when
narration: The Egedege dance originated in Unubi, Anambra State, Nigeria.
It is an interpretation of an older moonlight dance performed by youths, which was modernized and popularized in 1985 by Theresa Onuorah.
The name is derived from local slang for richness and bravery.

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Egedege is performed at Igbo cultural festivals, high-profile weddings, funerals, and official government events.
It symbolizes richness, bravery, and royal prestige.
Today it is a living tradition.

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: The performance begins with a flute cue heralding the group's entrance.
The lead 'queen' enters under a large umbrella, fanned by an attendant.
She leads the singing and dances to the rhythm of the instruments.
Watch for The Queen's Entrance.

scenes.title: Listen
narration: The music is driven by the ogene (metal gong), udu (pottery drum), ekwe (slit drum), and flutes.
The queen acts as the chief vocalist, often with backup singers.
Listen for the Ogene (metal gong), Udu, Ekwe, Flute.

The sound is defined by the sharp, resonant clanging of the ogene metal gong and the melodic, breathy calls of the flute. It features a call-and-response vocal structure led by a powerful female voice, supported by the deep earthy tones of the udu and ekwe drums.

scenes.title: The costume and the setting
narration: The queen wears a bronze crown with ostrich feathers, an elaborate robe with ten strings of waist beads, and carries a horsetail and bronze staff.
Dancers wear raffia waist shrouds, armbands, calf/ankle jingles, and red head ribbons.
The primary colors are red and white.

scenes.title: The people
narration: Theresa Onuorah is the central figure who created the modern version in 1985 and remains the leader of the Unubi Egedege dance group.
While originating in Unubi, modern variations exist among different artists, though they maintain the core traits of heavy traditional royal costumes and specific instrumentation.
The dance is a direct descendant of the traditional moonlight dances of the Unubi people, evolved into a professional performance art.
